title: Regular sequences and short exact sequences
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $0\to M_1\xrightarrow{\alpha}M_2\xrightarrow{\beta}M_3\to0$ a short exact sequence of $R$-modules and $f_1,\dots,f_r\in R$. For $0\le i\le r$ write $I_i=(f_1,\dots,f_i)\subset R$. (a) Suppose that for every $i=1,\dots,r$ the element $f_i$ is a nonzerodivisor on $M_1/I_{i-1}M_1$ and on $M_3/I_{i-1}M_3$ (condition (1) of [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence] for $M_1$ and for $M_3$). Then for every $i=1,\dots,r$ the element $f_i$ is a nonzerodivisor on $M_2/I_{i-1}M_2$, and for every $0\le i\le r$ the sequence $0\to M_1/I_iM_1\to M_2/I_iM_2\to M_3/I_iM_3\to0$ induced by $\alpha,\beta$ is exact. (b) Consequently, if $f_1,\dots,f_r$ is an $M_1$-regular sequence and an $M_3$-regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence], then it is an $M_2$-regular sequence.

proof.text: Induced maps and cokernels of multiplication. For an ideal $I\subset R$ one has $\alpha(IM_1)\subseteq IM_2$ and $\beta(IM_2)\subseteq IM_3$ (as $\alpha(xm)=x\alpha(m)$), so $\alpha,\beta$ induce $R$-linear maps $\alpha_I:M_1/IM_1\to M_2/IM_2$, $\beta_I:M_2/IM_2\to M_3/IM_3$ with $\beta_I\alpha_I=0$; for $I=I_0=0$ these are $\alpha,\beta$. Let $N$ be an $R$-module and $1\le i\le r$. Since $I_i=I_{i-1}+Rf_i$, we have $I_iN=I_{i-1}N+f_iN$, whose image in $N/I_{i-1}N$ is $f_i\cdot(N/I_{i-1}N)$; hence the cokernel of multiplication by $f_i$ on $N/I_{i-1}N$ is $(N/I_{i-1}N)/f_i(N/I_{i-1}N)=N/I_iN$, the quotient map being the projection $N/I_{i-1}N\to N/I_iN$. Under these identifications for $N=M_1,M_2,M_3$, the maps of cokernels induced by $\alpha_{I_{i-1}}$ and $\beta_{I_{i-1}}$ are $\alpha_{I_i}$ and $\beta_{I_i}$ (both send the class of $m$ to the class of $\alpha(m)$, resp. $\beta(m)$).

proof.text: The inductive claim. For $0\le i\le r$ let $(P_i)$ be: the sequence $0\to M_1/I_iM_1\xrightarrow{\alpha_{I_i}}M_2/I_iM_2\xrightarrow{\beta_{I_i}}M_3/I_iM_3\to0$ is exact, and $f_j$ is a nonzerodivisor on $M_2/I_{j-1}M_2$ for every $1\le j\le i$. $(P_0)$ holds: $I_0=0$, so the sequence is the given short exact sequence (Step 1), and the second condition is empty. We show $(P_{i-1})\Rightarrow(P_i)$ for $1\le i\le r$ in Step 3; then $(P_r)$ is part (a).

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0F1T (lemma-regular-sequence-short-exact-sequence), proof ('The lemma follows from this and induction on r. Some details omitted.'; the induction is set up here)

proof.text: The inductive step, by the snake lemma. Assume $(P_{i-1})$, $1\le i\le r$, and write $\bar M_j=M_j/I_{i-1}M_j$. Consider the commutative diagram whose two rows are both the exact sequence $0\to\bar M_1\xrightarrow{\alpha_{I_{i-1}}}\bar M_2\xrightarrow{\beta_{I_{i-1}}}\bar M_3\to0$ of $(P_{i-1})$ and whose three vertical maps are multiplication by $f_i$; it commutes because $\alpha_{I_{i-1}},\beta_{I_{i-1}}$ are $R$-linear. The top row has $\beta_{I_{i-1}}$ surjective and exactness at $\bar M_2$, the bottom row has $\alpha_{I_{i-1}}$ injective and exactness at $\bar M_2$, and moreover the top first map is injective and the bottom last map surjective. By the snake lemma [lem-weil-pbc-snake-lemma-modules] the sequence $\ker(f_i|\bar M_1)\to\ker(f_i|\bar M_2)\to\ker(f_i|\bar M_3)\xrightarrow{\partial}\operatorname{coker}(f_i|\bar M_1)\to\operatorname{coker}(f_i|\bar M_2)\to\operatorname{coker}(f_i|\bar M_3)$ is exact, its first map is injective and its last map surjective. By hypothesis $f_i$ is a nonzerodivisor on $\bar M_1$ and on $\bar M_3$, so $\ker(f_i|\bar M_1)=0=\ker(f_i|\bar M_3)$. Exactness at $\ker(f_i|\bar M_2)$ between two zero modules gives $\ker(f_i|\bar M_2)=0$: $f_i$ is a nonzerodivisor on $M_2/I_{i-1}M_2$. Exactness at $\operatorname{coker}(f_i|\bar M_1)$ with $\partial$ defined on $0$ gives that $\operatorname{coker}(f_i|\bar M_1)\to\operatorname{coker}(f_i|\bar M_2)$ is injective; with exactness at $\operatorname{coker}(f_i|\bar M_2)$ and surjectivity of the last map the three cokernels form a short exact sequence. By Step 1 the cokernels are $M_j/I_iM_j$ and the maps are $\alpha_{I_i},\beta_{I_i}$, so $0\to M_1/I_iM_1\to M_2/I_iM_2\to M_3/I_iM_3\to0$ is exact. With $(P_{i-1})$ for $j<i$ this is $(P_i)$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0F1T (lemma-regular-sequence-short-exact-sequence), proof ('By Lemma 07JW [lemma-snake], if f_1 : M_1 -> M_1 and f_1 : M_3 -> M_3 are injective, then so is f_1 : M_2 -> M_2 and we obtain a short exact sequence 0 -> M_1/f_1M_1 -> M_2/f_1M_2 -> M_3/f_1M_3 -> 0', applied to the modules M_j/I_{i-1}M_j)

proof.text: Part (b). Suppose $f_1,\dots,f_r$ is $M_1$-regular and $M_3$-regular [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence]. Condition (1) of the definition for $M_1$ and $M_3$ is the hypothesis of (a), so by (a) (Steps 2 and 3) $f_i$ is a nonzerodivisor on $M_2/I_{i-1}M_2$ for $i=1,\dots,r$: condition (1) for $M_2$. By (a) $\beta_{I_r}:M_2/I_rM_2\to M_3/I_rM_3$ is surjective, and $M_3/I_rM_3\neq0$ by condition (2) for $M_3$; hence $M_2/I_rM_2\neq0$, condition (2) for $M_2$. So $f_1,\dots,f_r$ is $M_2$-regular.
